title: Adapter and Bridge
scopeHtml: Scope: Adapter (object vs class), Bridge, class diagrams, before/after refactors, when not to use, JDK/Retrofit/JDBC examples. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: Why structural patterns exist
notes.html:
Structural patterns are about how classes and objects are glued together into bigger structures. Creational patterns answer "how do I make it", behavioral ones answer "how do they talk", structural ones answer "how are the pieces shaped and connected". The seven you must know: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy.

The common trick behind all of them: instead of changing a class, you put another object next to it or around it and use composition (holding a reference) instead of inheritance. Composition can be swapped at runtime; inheritance is frozen at compile time.

Worked example. A payments app has 3 gateways (Stripe, Razorpay, PayPal) and 2 channels (web, mobile). With inheritance you would write 3 x 2 = 6 classes; with composition 3 + 2 = 5, and a fourth gateway costs 1 class, not 2. That arithmetic is the whole argument for Bridge.

Industry examples. Java IO (BufferedInputStream wraps FileInputStream), Android RecyclerView.Adapter, OkHttp interceptors, Retrofit's generated API objects, Servlet filters: all structural patterns in everyday libraries.

Everyday analogy. Travel plug adapters, a gift wrapped in paper, a folder inside a folder: you do not rebuild the thing, you add a shape around it.

Common interview traps.

  • Naming a pattern without saying what problem it solves.
  • Confusing Adapter, Decorator, Proxy: all three wrap one object. The difference is intent (see the comparison file).
  • Forgetting that "prefer composition over inheritance" is the underlying principle.

notes.title: Adapter: the idea
notes.html:
An Adapter makes an existing class fit an interface the client expects, without changing either side. You own the client, you do not own (or do not want to touch) the library. The adapter translates calls.

Mechanism: the adapter implements the target interface and holds the adaptee. Each target method calls the adaptee's method(s), converting arguments and results.

+-----------+      uses      +-----------------+
|  Client   | -------------> | <<Target>>      |
+-----------+                | + pay(rupees)   |
                             +--------+--------+
                                      ^
                                      | implements
                             +--------+--------+      has-a      +------------------+
                             | StripeAdapter   | -------------->  | StripeSdk        |
                             | - sdk           |                  | + charge(cents,  |
                             | + pay(rupees)   |                  |    currency)     |
                             +-----------------+                  +------------------+

Worked example. Your app calls pay(499.0) in rupees. The Stripe SDK wants charge(long amountInMinorUnits, String currency). The adapter does sdk.charge(Math.round(499.0 * 100), "inr") so 49,900 paise reach Stripe. One bug here (using 499 instead of 49,900) means customers pay 1 percent of the price, which is why this conversion lives in exactly one class.

Industry examples. Arrays.asList(array) adapts an array to the List interface. InputStreamReader adapts a byte stream (InputStream) to a character stream (Reader). Android RecyclerView.Adapter adapts your data list to views. Retrofit CallAdapter turns a Call<T> into Single<T>, Flow or a coroutine.

Everyday analogy. A travel plug adapter: the wall socket and your laptop charger are both fine, they just disagree on shape.

Decision gravity. Cheap and reversible: an adapter is a small class and removing it later is a local change. It becomes a one-way door only if the adapter's interface leaks library types everywhere.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying the adapter "changes" the adaptee. It never does.
  • Putting business logic in the adapter; it should only translate.
  • Not mentioning Adapter is the standard shield against vendor lock-in.

notes.title: Adapter in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before (no pattern). Every call site talks to the vendor SDK directly. Swapping vendors means editing 40 files.

// BEFORE: SDK types and cents conversion leak into business code
class CheckoutService {
    private final StripeSdk stripe = new StripeSdk();
    void checkout(double rupees) {
        stripe.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr"); // repeated in every caller
    }
}

After (object adapter).

interface PaymentGateway { boolean pay(double rupees); }

class StripeSdk {                              // third-party, cannot edit
    boolean charge(long minorUnits, String currency) { return minorUnits > 0; }
}

class StripeAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final StripeSdk sdk;
    StripeAdapter(StripeSdk sdk) { this.sdk = sdk; }
    @Override public boolean pay(double rupees) {
        return sdk.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr");
    }
}

class CheckoutService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;          // depends on the abstraction
    CheckoutService(PaymentGateway g) { this.gateway = g; }
    void checkout(double rupees) { gateway.pay(rupees); }
}

Kotlin variant, plus an extension-function alternative:

interface PaymentGateway { fun pay(rupees: Double): Boolean }

class StripeAdapter(private val sdk: StripeSdk) : PaymentGateway {
    override fun pay(rupees: Double) = sdk.charge(Math.round(rupees * 100), "inr")
}

// Kotlin shortcut: delegation lets you adapt and reuse the rest for free
class LoggingGateway(inner: PaymentGateway) : PaymentGateway by inner

Object vs class adapter. Object adapter (above) uses composition, works in Java and Kotlin, and can adapt subclasses of the adaptee. Class adapter extends the adaptee and implements the target; it needs multiple inheritance, so in Java it works only if the target is an interface. Prefer the object adapter.

Common interview traps.

  • Writing a class adapter and then being unable to explain why it breaks when the adaptee is final.
  • Mixing up the direction: the adapter implements the interface the CLIENT wants, not the library's.

notes.title: Adapter: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not adapt when you own both sides and can simply change one. An adapter between two of your own classes is a sign the design drifted; fix the interface instead.

Skip it when the two interfaces are already nearly identical (one method rename). A thin adapter that only renames is noise, and each extra layer adds a stack frame and a place for bugs.

Do not let it grow into a god translator that also validates, retries and logs. That is Facade or Decorator work.

Worked example. A team wrapped Retrofit in ApiAdapter, wrapped by ApiService, wrapped by ApiRepository, all with the same method names. 3 layers, 0 translation, +1 file to touch per new endpoint (about 15 minutes lost per endpoint across a year of 80 endpoints = 20 hours).

Common interview traps.

  • "Always wrap third-party libraries." Wrap the ones likely to change or leak types; wrapping String helpers is silly.
  • Not noticing a 1:1 wrapper adds no value.

notes.title: Bridge: the idea
notes.html:
Bridge splits one class hierarchy into two independent ones, an abstraction and an implementation, linked by composition so each can vary alone. It prevents the "class explosion" of 2 dimensions of variation.

Mechanism: the abstraction holds a reference to an implementor interface. Subclasses of the abstraction add higher-level behavior; subclasses of the implementor supply low-level operations.

 Abstraction side                       Implementor side
+------------------+   has-a   +---------------------+
| Notification     | --------> | <<MessageSender>>   |
| + send(text)     |           | + deliver(text)     |
+--------+---------+           +----------+----------+
         ^                                ^
   +-----+------+                  +------+-------+------+
   |            |                  |              |      |
 Urgent     Digest             SmsSender   EmailSender  PushSender

Worked example. 3 notification types (Urgent, Digest, Marketing) x 4 channels (SMS, Email, Push, WhatsApp) = 12 classes with inheritance. With Bridge: 3 + 4 = 7. Add a 5th channel: +1 class, not +3. At 10 types x 10 channels the numbers are 100 vs 20.

Industry examples. JDBC: DriverManager/Connection is the abstraction, each database vendor's driver is an implementor. Android's View draws through a Canvas abstraction with different backends (software vs hardware). SLF4J is a facade-plus-bridge: your code uses the SLF4J API, bindings choose Logback or Log4j (treat the exact classification as a discussion point, it is both).

Everyday analogy. A TV remote (abstraction: basic remote, smart remote) and the TV brand (implementor: Sony, Samsung). You can upgrade the remote without changing the TV and vice versa.

Decision gravity. Costs more up front than Adapter. It is a design-time decision, so retrofitting is a refactor (moderately reversible). Worth it only when you truly see two axes growing.

Common interview traps.

  • Mixing up Bridge and Adapter: Adapter fixes a mismatch AFTER the fact; Bridge is planned UP FRONT to keep two axes separate.
  • Calling every interface-with-implementations a Bridge. Bridge needs two hierarchies.

notes.title: Bridge in code: before and after
notes.html:
Before. Inheritance explosion:

// BEFORE: one class per combination
class UrgentSmsNotification {}
class UrgentEmailNotification {}
class DigestSmsNotification {}
class DigestEmailNotification {}
// ... 12 classes, copy-pasted delivery code

After.

interface MessageSender { void deliver(String to, String body); }
class SmsSender implements MessageSender {
    public void deliver(String to, String body) { System.out.println("SMS " + to + ": " + body); }
}
class EmailSender implements MessageSender {
    public void deliver(String to, String body) { System.out.println("MAIL " + to + ": " + body); }
}

abstract class Notification {
    protected final MessageSender sender;          // the bridge
    Notification(MessageSender s) { this.sender = s; }
    abstract void notifyUser(String user, String text);
}
class UrgentNotification extends Notification {
    UrgentNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser(String u, String t) { sender.deliver(u, "[URGENT] " + t); }
}
class DigestNotification extends Notification {
    DigestNotification(MessageSender s) { super(s); }
    void notifyUser(String u, String t) { sender.deliver(u, "Daily digest: " + t); }
}

// new UrgentNotification(new SmsSender()).notifyUser("+91-98...", "Server down");
fun interface MessageSender { fun deliver(to: String, body: String) }

abstract class Notification(protected val sender: MessageSender) {
    abstract fun notifyUser(user: String, text: String)
}
class UrgentNotification(s: MessageSender) : Notification(s) {
    override fun notifyUser(user: String, text: String) = sender.deliver(user, "[URGENT] $text")
}
// Kotlin: a SAM lambda is a sender
val sms = MessageSender { to, body -> println("SMS $to: $body") }

Common interview traps.

  • Using inheritance in the abstraction side only and forgetting that the implementor must be injected (constructor), otherwise you cannot swap at runtime.
  • Not being able to produce the class-count arithmetic when asked "why".

notes.title: Bridge: when NOT to use it
notes.html:
Do not use it when there is only one axis of variation. One axis is plain Strategy or an interface, with no second hierarchy to bridge.

Do not use it when the second axis will never grow (for example "we will only ever send email"). You pay indirection for nothing.

It is easy to over-apply to small apps; two classes and an if are fine until the third combination appears.

Worked example. A report exporter with 1 report type and 3 formats is just Strategy (3 + 1 classes). Add a second report dimension (PDF vs dashboard layout) with 4 more formats, and now Bridge pays: 2 + 4 = 6 instead of 8.

Common interview traps.

  • Choosing Bridge when Strategy is enough; both use composition, but Bridge has a hierarchy on each side.
  • Forgetting that Bridge is about structure, Strategy is about swapping an algorithm.

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• Structural patterns glue objects by composition: Adapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy.
  • Adapter translates an existing class to the interface the client wants; use an object adapter; keep it logic-free; do not wrap what you own.
  • Real examples: Arrays.asList, InputStreamReader, RecyclerView.Adapter, Retrofit CallAdapter.
  • Bridge separates two axes (abstraction x implementation) so classes grow as A + B, not A x B.
  • Real examples: JDBC drivers, View/Canvas, logging bindings.
  • Adapter fixes mismatch afterwards; Bridge prevents it up front.
  • Avoid both when there is no real mismatch or only one axis of variation.
